content: 1. Stakeholders at various levels must consider the costs and opportunities for cost savings, the shelf-life of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs, the risk of stock-outs if procurement does not meet demand, and the risk of expired health products if quantities procured are overestimated. 2. National HIV programs should establish a stakeholder working group to address these issues, involving health policymakers, implementers, procurement and supply management (PSM) specialists, representatives from central medical stores management, and the finance ministry. 3. Medicines should be selected based on national antiretroviral therapy (ART) guidelines and program needs, such as choosing between lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) and atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r), or between lamivudine (3TC)-containing and emtricitabine (FTC)-containing formulations. 4. It is recommended to minimize the overall number of ARV drug regimens to optimize treatment and sourcing. WHO surveys indicate that 30% of reporting countries use over 10 different first-line ARV regimens for adults and adolescents. 5. Before including new products in national essential medicines lists, their registration and intellectual property status should be verified to ensure they can be imported. 6. If a selected ARV drug is not on the national list or registered in the country, HIV program managers should coordinate with the national drug regulatory authority to have these drugs listed and registered. Pharmaceutical companies also have a responsibility to register their products in countries where they market them. 7. Drugs no longer recommended by WHO for any ARV treatment regimen should be removed from national ART guidelines and essential medicines lists. Plans should be made to transition patients to more effective regimens, using existing stocks appropriately. 8. The synchronized introduction of new guidelines with planning for forecasting, procurement, and distribution will minimize waste of phased-out products and shortages of newly recommended products. 9. Quantification of needs should be conducted annually, projecting for at least two years, with quarterly or semi-annual reviews to adjust for significant changes in demand. 10. PSM managers should plan ahead and place long-term orders while maintaining flexibility to adjust for changes in scale-up pace, regimen switching, or unforeseen events affecting consumption. 11. Procurement managers should develop a supply plan that accounts for current stock levels, existing orders, available budgets, required new orders, safety buffer stock, and delivery dates for new shipments. 12. A uniform and harmonized procurement system is essential to efficiently procure quality-assured, affordable ARV drugs and diagnostics. Transparent procedures should be adopted to achieve best-value procurement, and a quality assurance system should be implemented for storage and distribution. 13. National procurement programs should consolidate PSM systems, pool procurement for ARV drugs and diagnostics, and consider joining pooled procurement mechanisms to increase economies of scale and minimize risks of long delivery times. 14. Long-term framework contracts should be established to allow call-down orders for regularly demanded commodities, reducing procurement transaction costs and fostering collaborative relationships between buyers and suppliers. 15. A multi-supplier procurement strategy should be implemented to support a healthy market and avoid dependence on a single supplier, ensuring flexibility during supply constraints or logistical difficulties. 16. Publicly accessible databases should be used to facilitate access to price information and support competition. 17. Storage and distribution of HIV medicines, diagnostics, and other commodities must be planned to accommodate increased volumes due to expanded ART coverage. This may require new public facilities or outsourcing to private sector facilities, provided they meet pharmaceutical storage standards. 18. Storage and distribution plans should include quality assurance of products upon receipt, secure storage facilities, cold storage for temperature-sensitive products, rationalization of storage levels, inventory control systems, regular distribution patterns, and routine data reporting to monitor usage and adjust for changes in consumption patterns. 19. To avoid stock-outs and expired health products, close coordination with HIV program managers and policymakers is essential to align treatment scale-up with commodity availability. 20. Quantification and ordering should include a rotating safety buffer to compensate for forecasting errors and delivery delays. This buffer should be part of normal stock rotation to avoid retaining aged or expiring products. 21. Orders should be placed at least six months in advance of the required delivery date to allow adequate time for production and cost-effective shipping. 22. Staged deliveries are recommended to provide flexible delivery schedules and optimize existing storage and distribution capacity. 23. PSM managers should be aware of potential global market constraints, such as shortages of active pharmaceutical ingredients, and factor these into delivery timelines. 24. Special consideration should be given to low-demand products, such as secondor third-line ART drugs and pediatric regimens, which may require pooled procurement and higher buffer stocks to compensate for less frequent production and delivery. 25. Robust information systems are critical to ensure accurate and timely consumption data for ARV drugs and diagnostics, enabling effective monitoring of the supply system and forecasting needs. 26. Monitoring PSM through early warning indicators prevents stock-outs and overstocking, which can lead to product expiry. 27. Reliable data capture and analysis from facilities support a bottom-up approach to quantification and forecasting, reflecting changes in demand and enabling flexible implementation of new recommendations. 28. Regimens containing nevirapine (NVP) are retained as an alternative option for patients who cannot tolerate or have contraindications to tenofovir (TDF) or efavirenz (EFV). 29. The supply chain faces challenges due to increased demand for preferred first-line fixed-dose combination (FDC) formulations, requiring careful planning and buffer stock maintenance to avoid supply constraints. 30. Delivery lead times for recommended first-line drugs may become extended during peak demand periods, necessitating proactive planning by PSM managers. 31. Purchasers and implementing partners must coordinate to ensure timely procurement and delivery of ARV drugs and diagnostics, avoiding delays and ensuring program flexibility.
